objects.name: Active Directory Takeover by Criminal Gang — Canadian Energy Sector
objects.description: A financially motivated criminal gang targets a mid-sized Canadian energy operator (~2500 employees). The campaign begins with a spearphishing lure crafted around energy-sector themes (e.g., regulatory filings, NERC CIP compliance documents), establishes a foothold via a commodity loader, pivots through credential harvesting and Kerberos abuse, and ultimately seizes control of Active Directory to deploy ransomware across OT-adjacent infrastructure.

objects.name: Spearphishing Attachment — Energy-Themed Lure
objects.description: Attackers send targeted emails to IT and finance staff impersonating a Canadian energy regulator (e.g., Canada Energy Regulator or IESO) with a macro-enabled Excel or Word attachment. The lure references a familiar compliance or procurement process to increase click likelihood in a 2500-person energy org where such communications are routine.

objects.name: User Execution — Malicious Office Macro
objects.description: A targeted employee opens the attachment and enables macros, executing an embedded VBA script that drops and runs a commodity loader (e.g., QakBot, IcedID, or Emotet — all historically used against energy sector targets). This gives the attacker an initial beacon on a domain-joined workstation.

objects.name: OS Credential Dumping — LSASS Memory
objects.description: After establishing persistence and disabling local AV, the attacker uses a Mimikatz-style tool or the loader's built-in credential harvesting module to dump plaintext credentials and NTLM hashes from LSASS on the initial workstation. This typically yields at minimum one domain user credential.

objects.name: Domain Account Discovery
objects.description: Using harvested credentials, the attacker enumerates Active Directory to identify privileged accounts (Domain Admins, Service Accounts, Tier-0 assets) via LDAP queries or BloodHound. In a 2500-person energy org this typically reveals a moderately complex AD structure with dedicated OT/SCADA-adjacent service accounts.

objects.name: Kerberoasting — Service Account Hash Extraction
objects.description: The attacker requests Kerberos TGS tickets for service accounts (common in energy orgs for historian, SCADA, or backup service accounts) and extracts the ticket hashes for offline cracking. Weak or default service account passwords in OT-adjacent environments frequently yield DA-level credentials.

objects.name: Lateral Movement via Pass-the-Hash to IT Admin Jump Host
objects.description: Using cracked or harvested NTLM hashes, the attacker authenticates to an IT administrator jump host or Tier-1 management server. In mid-sized energy organisations, these jump hosts often bridge corporate IT and OT network segments and run with elevated AD privileges.

objects.name: Remote Services — RDP to Domain Controller
objects.description: From the privileged jump host, the attacker uses RDP with Domain Admin credentials (now in hand) to connect directly to one of the organisation's Domain Controllers. Energy sector DCs often run additional roles (DNS, NPS) and are highly valuable targets.

objects.name: DCSync — Domain Credential Replication
objects.description: With Domain Admin rights on the DC, the attacker performs a DCSync attack using Mimikatz's lsadump::dcsync, pulling NTLM hashes for all accounts including KRBTGT — enabling full Golden Ticket capability. This constitutes complete Active Directory takeover.

objects.name: Create/Modify Domain Account — Backdoor Admin
objects.description: The attacker creates a hidden Domain Admin account with a benign-sounding name (e.g., matching naming conventions for IT service accounts) to ensure persistent AD access even if the initial compromise path is remediated. This is consistent with ransomware gang TTPs that maintain access during negotiation.

objects.name: Inhibit System Recovery — Shadow Copy Deletion via GPO
objects.description: Using Domain Admin access, the attacker deploys a malicious GPO to all domain-joined machines that deletes Volume Shadow Copies (vssadmin delete shadows) and disables Windows Recovery Environment, preventing easy restoration before ransomware detonation.

objects.name: Data Encrypted for Impact — Ransomware Deployment via GPO
objects.description: The attacker pushes ransomware (e.g., BlackCat/ALPHV, Play, or LockBit 3.0 — all observed in energy sector incidents) to all domain-joined endpoints via Group Policy startup scripts or PSEXEC from the DC, maximising encryption coverage across the 2500-person organisation. OT historian servers and engineering workstations on the corporate domain are particularly targeted to maximise leverage.

objects.name: Energy management and NERC CIP compliance systems
